standard_text: Solve equations of the form px + q = r and p(x + q) = r fluently, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Represent real-world problems using equations of these forms and solve such problems.

progression.narrative:
This standard asks seventh graders to solve two families of linear equation -- px + q = r and p(x + q) = r -- fluently with rational numbers, and then to use those equations to model and solve real-world problems. 'Fluently' is the load-bearing word: students should run a dependable procedure, not reinvent it each time. So the progression starts with the pure mechanic. First, the two-step equation px + q = r: undo the operations in reverse order, clearing the added or subtracted constant before dividing by the coefficient -- and checking the answer by substituting it back. Next, the parenthetical form p(x + q) = r, where students learn two equivalent routes (divide by p first, or distribute p across the parentheses) and confront the classic trap of multiplying only the first term inside. The 'fluently, with rational numbers' demand runs through both, so the difficulty climbs from integers to a single fraction or decimal.

With the solving machinery in hand, the standard turns outward to modeling. Students first learn to IDENTIFY the equation that matches a situation -- giving every number a job, with the per-unit rate multiplying the variable and the one-time amount added on its own -- before they WRITE and solve their own, first with whole numbers and then with rational values (the baker's fractions, the shopper's decimals). The top of the progression stretches into representing one situation with more than one equivalent equation, comparing an algebraic solve to an arithmetic one, and judging whether a solution is reasonable. The order is deliberate: solve px + q = r, then p(x + q) = r, then identify, write, and finally represent-multiple-ways -- and underneath all of it runs one habit we keep returning to, that every legal move keeps the equation balanced and the answer isn't finished until a substitution proves it true. (Note: unlike eighth grade, the variable inside the parentheses always has a coefficient of 1 -- there is no p(ax + q), no combining like terms, and no variables on both sides.)

steps.rationale: The mechanical core: solve a two-step equation px + q = r by undoing operations in reverse order. This is the Below-proficiency task and the procedure every later step relies on.

The standard's second equation form, p(x + q) = r, adds the parentheses. Students need a reliable route (divide first or distribute) and must multiply every term inside -- a distinct mechanic worth its own step.
Before writing an equation from scratch, students identify which equation matches a situation, mapping each number to its job. Recognizing the model is a separate skill from executing it.
The At-proficiency demand: write AND solve a real-world equation, first with whole numbers. Building the equation (often p(x + q) = r for a whole group) is distinct from solving it.
The same modeling with rational values (fractions and decimals), where the 'fluently, with rational numbers' demand bites -- students must finish by dividing out a fraction or decimal coefficient.
The Above-proficiency payoff: model one situation with more than one equivalent equation, compare algebraic and arithmetic methods, and judge whether a solution is reasonable.

skills.name: Solve one-step equations using inverse operations

prerequisite_skill.description: Understand that an equation is balanced and that operations undo each other.

skills.i_do_script: A one-step equation has just one thing happening to the variable, and I undo it with the opposite operation. Watch: x + 6 = 10. Six is ADDED to x, so I subtract 6 from BOTH sides: x = 4. Another: 3x = 21. Here x is MULTIPLIED by 3, so I divide both sides by 3: x = 7. Addition undoes subtraction; multiplication undoes division. Whatever I do to one side I do to the other so the equation stays balanced.

canonical_error.pattern: Uses the same operation shown in the equation instead of its inverse
canonical_error.example: For x + 6 = 10 the student ADDS 6 to get x = 16, instead of subtracting 6
canonical_error.why: The student repeats the operation they see rather than undoing it. To isolate x you apply the INVERSE operation to both sides.

skills.item_template: A one-step equation (x + q = r, x - q = r, px = r, or x/p = r) with rational values. Student isolates x. Short numeric response; good fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: Solve x + 7 = 12.
Solve x - 4 = 9.
Solve 3x = 21.
Solve x/5 = 4.
Solve x + 3.5 = 8.
Solve 6x = 15.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- do the OPPOSITE, not the same.
redirect_script.prompt: Ask what is happening to x: is it added, subtracted, multiplied, or divided? Do the inverse to BOTH sides. Added six? Subtract six.
redirect_script.praise: You undid the operation with its inverse -- that isolates x.

vocabulary.definition: A math sentence saying two expressions are equal, with an = sign.
The operation that undoes another: subtraction undoes addition, division undoes multiplication.
Get the variable alone on one side of the equation.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'x - 8 = 5.'
What is happening to x?
8 is subtracted from x, so I add 8 to both sides: x = 13.
If the student subtracts 8, ask 'does subtracting again undo a subtraction?'
Your turn: 4x = 20. What is the inverse of times 4?

skills.name: Compute fluently with rational numbers (fractions and decimals)

prerequisite_skill.description: Add, subtract, multiply, and divide fractions and decimals.

skills.i_do_script: Solving equations with rational numbers means I have to add, subtract, multiply, and divide fractions and decimals without freezing up. Watch a division that surprises people: 12 divided by 0.5. Dividing by one-half is the same as multiplying by 2, so 12 / 0.5 = 24 -- the answer gets BIGGER. And 9 / 1.5 = 6. With fractions, two-thirds of 9 is (2/3) x 9 = 6. A calculator is allowed on this standard, so the goal is knowing WHICH operation to do and trusting the result.

canonical_error.pattern: Assumes dividing always makes a number smaller (or multiplying always bigger), mishandling division by a number less than 1
canonical_error.example: Thinks 12 / 0.5 = 6 because 'dividing makes it smaller,' instead of 24
canonical_error.why: The student over-generalizes whole-number intuition. Dividing by a number between 0 and 1 makes the result LARGER; the operation, not the size, decides.

skills.item_template: A single rational-number computation (fraction or decimal) of the kind that appears while solving. Short numeric response; fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: Compute 12 / 0.5.
Compute 7.5 - 3.
Compute (1/2) x 8.
Compute 15 - 1.5.
Compute 9 / 1.5.
Compute (2/3) x 9.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on -- check that with the calculator.
redirect_script.prompt: Ask: am I dividing by a number LESS than 1? If so, the answer grows. Estimate first: 12 split into halves gives 24 halves.
redirect_script.praise: You trusted the math over the 'dividing shrinks' myth -- exactly right.

vocabulary.definition: Any number that can be written as a fraction of integers, including decimals and whole numbers.
Working accurately and efficiently, without getting stuck on the arithmetic.

worked_example_script.text: Is 0.25 bigger or smaller than 1?
Smaller, so the answer grows: dividing by one-fourth is timesing by 4, so 8 / 0.25 = 32.
If the student writes 2, ask 'how many quarters are in 8?'
Your turn: (3/4) x 8.

skills.name: Solve two-step equations of the form px + q = r
skills.i_do_script: A two-step equation has TWO things happening to x, and I undo them in reverse order -- like taking off shoes before socks. Watch the spec's example: 3x - 6 = 27. The x is multiplied by 3, then 6 is subtracted. I clear the subtraction FIRST: add 6 to both sides, giving 3x = 33. Then I undo the multiplication: divide both sides by 3, giving x = 11. I finish by checking: 3(11) - 6 = 33 - 6 = 27. It works, so x = 11.

canonical_error.pattern: Undoes the multiplication before clearing the added or subtracted constant
canonical_error.example: For 3x - 6 = 27 the student divides by 3 first (getting x - 2 = 9) instead of adding 6 first
canonical_error.why: The student attacks the coefficient before the constant, following left-to-right habits instead of reverse order of operations. The added/subtracted term must be cleared before the multiplication is undone.

skills.item_template: A two-step equation px + q = r with integer (or simple rational) values. Student isolates x. MC or short numeric response.

sample_items.stem:
An equation is given.

  3x - 6 = 27

What is the solution to the equation?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Add 6 (33), divide by 3 -> 11. '7' comes from 21/3 (subtracting wrong); '36' keeps 3x = 36 without dividing; '66' doubles instead of dividing.

sample_items.stem:
An equation is given.

  4x + 5 = 25

What is the solution to the equation?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Subtract 5 (20), divide by 4 -> 5. '6.25' divides 25/4 without clearing +5; '7.5' uses 30/4; '100' multiplies.

sample_items.stem: Solve 7x - 3 = 18.
Solve 2x + 5 = 17.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- what is done to x LAST?
redirect_script.prompt: Undo in reverse: clear the added or subtracted number FIRST (do the opposite to both sides), and only THEN divide by the number multiplying x. Underline the constant and deal with it first.
redirect_script.praise: You cleared the constant before touching the coefficient -- that's the right order.

vocabulary.definition: An equation that needs two inverse operations to solve, like 3x - 6 = 27.
The number multiplied by the variable, like the 3 in 3x.
A plain number with no variable, like the -6 in 3x - 6.

worked_example_script.text: Write '5x + 2 = 17.'
What two things are happening to x, and in what order?
x is times 5, then + 2. Clear the +2 first: subtract 2 to get 5x = 15. Then divide by 5: x = 3.
If the student divides by 5 first, ask 'what number is added to the 5x? Clear that first.'
Your turn: 3x - 6 = 27. Which do you undo first?

practice_problems.stem: Solve x + 4 = 10.
In 3x - 6 = 27, which do you undo first: the '- 6' or the 'times 3'?
Solve 3x - 6 = 27.
practice_problems.notes: The spec's Below example; add 6, then divide by 3.

practice_problems.stem: Solve 4x + 5 = 25.
Alex solved 2x + 8 = 20. Find and fix the mistake.
practice_problems.answer: Alex divided by 2 before clearing the + 8. Clear the constant first: 2x = 12, then divide by 2 to get x = 6. Check: 2(6) + 8 = 20.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: dividing before subtracting.

practice_problems.stem: Solve 7x - 3 = 18.
Solve 4x + 3 = 1.
practice_problems.notes: Rational, negative solution: 4x = -2.

practice_problems.stem: Write a two-step equation of the form px + q = r whose solution is x = 4. Show your check.
practice_problems.notes: Reverse direction -- build an equation with a known solution.

activities.title: Which Step First?
materials: Card set: 8 equations (some one-step, some two-step)
activities.instructions:
1. Each card shows an equation like 3x - 6 = 27.
2. Decide the FIRST move: 'Add or subtract first' or 'Divide first.'
3. Sort every card -- a two-step equation always clears the constant first; a one-step (like 5x = 30) only divides.
4. Then solve three cards and check by substituting back.
5. Debrief: what goes wrong if you divide before clearing the constant?

activities.title: Order Detective
activities.instructions:
1. Read Alex's solution to 2x + 8 = 20.
2. Circle the exact line where Alex undid the wrong operation first.
3. Redo the solve in the correct order and check your answer.
4. Write the rule: which do you always clear first -- the constant or the coefficient?

content.worked_problem: 2x + 8 = 20. Alex divided by 2 first and got x = 2.
content.error_step: Alex divided by 2 before clearing the + 8.
content.why: Clear the added constant first: 2x = 12, then divide by 2 to get x = 6.

strategy_links.why: Two-step solving is a fixed procedure; gradual release adds one inverse-operation move at a time before independent practice.
The divide-before-subtract slip is a precise, baitable error ideal for find-and-fix.
Choral response on 'clear the constant first, then divide' hard-wires the reverse-order habit.

questioning_prompts: What two things are happening to x, and in what order?
Which do you undo first -- and why that one?
What do you get after you clear the constant?
How can you check that your answer is right?
Where would dividing too early show up in your answer?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student divides by the coefficient before clearing the added or subtracted constant.
misconception_redirects.say: Undo in reverse: clear the added or subtracted number FIRST (do the opposite to both sides), and only THEN divide by the number multiplying x. Underline the constant and deal with it first.
misconception_redirects.praise: You cleared the constant before touching the coefficient -- that's the right order.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student changes only one side of the equation.
misconception_redirects.say: Whatever you do to one side, do to the other. Write the '+ 6' under BOTH sides so the equation stays balanced.
misconception_redirects.praise: You kept both sides balanced -- that's what keeps the equation true.

quick_checks.look_for: x = 3 (subtract 2, then divide by 5). Dividing first (17/5 = 3.4) signals the order error.
x = 3 (add 1, then divide by 4). An answer of 2.75 means the student divided before adding.

sentence_starters: First I undo the ___ by ___ing both sides, which gives ___.
Then I divide both sides by ___ to get x = ___.

steps.annotation: Two operations on x: times 2, then + 5.
Clear the added constant first, on both sides.
Undo the multiplication last.
Substitute back -- both sides match, so x = 6.
Two operations: times 4, then - 7.
Clear the constant first (add 7 to both sides).
Divide both sides by 4 to isolate x.
Check by substituting your answer into the original.

skills.name: Solve equations of the form p(x + q) = r
skills.i_do_script: When the variable sits inside parentheses, p(x + q) = r, I have two good routes. Watch the spec's example: 0.5(x - 3) = 7.5. Route 1 -- divide first: divide both sides by 0.5 to get x - 3 = 15, then add 3 to get x = 18. Route 2 -- distribute first: 0.5 times x is 0.5x and 0.5 times -3 is -1.5, giving 0.5x - 1.5 = 7.5, then add 1.5 and divide by 0.5 to get x = 18. Both land on x = 18. The trap in distributing is forgetting to multiply the SECOND number inside, so I say both products out loud.

canonical_error.pattern: Distributes p to the variable only, forgetting to multiply the constant inside the parentheses
canonical_error.example: For 0.5(x - 3) = 7.5 the student writes 0.5x - 3 = 7.5 (never multiplied -3 by 0.5) instead of 0.5x - 1.5 = 7.5
canonical_error.why: The student treats the outside factor as attached to just the first term. The distributive property multiplies EVERY term inside: p(x + q) = px + pq. Missing the second product corrupts the solve.

skills.item_template: An equation p(x + q) = r with rational p, q, r (at least one may be a fraction or decimal). Student solves by dividing first or distributing first. Numeric response.

sample_items.stem:
An equation is given.

  0.5(x - 3) = 7.5

What is the solution to the equation?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Divide by 0.5 -> x - 3 = 15, add 3 -> 18. Distributing to only the first term (0.5x - 3 = 7.5) would give x = 21.

sample_items.stem: Solve 3(x + 5) = 27.

redirect_script.stop: Did the outside number reach BOTH terms?
redirect_script.prompt: If you distribute, draw an arrow from the outside number to EACH term inside and say both products aloud. If you divide first, divide the whole right side by p before you touch the parentheses.
redirect_script.praise: You multiplied both terms (or divided the whole side) -- that's a clean parenthesis solve.

vocabulary.definition: a(b + c) = ab + ac: the number outside the parentheses multiplies each term inside.
An equation where the variable is only to the first power, like 0.5(x - 3) = 7.5.
Solving accurately and efficiently, choosing an efficient route.

worked_example_script.text: What are your two routes here?
Divide first: x + 3 = 8, so x = 5. Or distribute: 4x + 12 = 32, 4x = 20, x = 5. Same answer.
If a student writes 4x + 3 = 32, ask 'did the 4 reach the 3 inside?'
Your turn, both ways: 2(x + 6) = 20.

practice_problems.stem: Distribute: 3(x + 4).
Solve 2(x + 1) = 10.

practice_problems.notes: Spec's Approaching example; divide by 0.5 or distribute.

practice_problems.stem: Solve 3(x + 5) = 27.
Morgan solved 4(x + 2) = 28. Find and fix the mistake.
practice_problems.answer: Morgan multiplied the 4 by x but not by the 2. It should be 4x + 8 = 28, so 4x = 20 and x = 5. Check: 4(5 + 2) = 4(7) = 28.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: distributed to the first term only.
Decimal coefficient; dividing by 2.5 first is cleanest.

practice_problems.stem: Solve 3(x - 2) = 9 two ways -- divide first, then distribute first -- and show both give the same answer.
practice_problems.answer: x = 5. Divide: x - 2 = 3, x = 5. Distribute: 3x - 6 = 9, 3x = 15, x = 5.
practice_problems.notes: Compares the two methods (previews the Above-band task).

activities.title: Fold and Unfold
materials: Card set: 6 p(x + q) cards and 8 expanded-form cards (two skip-the-second-term decoys)
activities.instructions:
1. Lay out the folded-form cards and the expanded-form cards.
2. Match each p(x + q) to its correct expansion.
3. Two expanded cards are decoys that skipped or mis-signed the second term -- set them aside and name the error.
4. To claim a match, say both products out loud.
5. Debrief: which term is the one people forget to multiply?

activities.title: Reach the Second Term
activities.instructions:
1. Read Morgan's solve of 4(x + 2) = 28 that starts '4x + 2 = 28.'
2. Circle the term the 4 never reached.
3. Rewrite the correct first line and finish the solve.
4. Write the one rule that fixes this error forever.

content.error_step: Morgan multiplied 4 by x but not by the 2 inside.
content.why: Distribute to every term: 4(x + 2) = 4x + 8, so 4x + 8 = 28 and x = 5.

strategy_links.why: An area/box model for distribution makes 'every term inside gets multiplied' concrete before the abstract rule.
The skip-the-second-term error is precise and baitable -- ideal for find-and-fix.
Thinking aloud 'p times x AND p times q' models the discipline that prevents the missed product.

questioning_prompts: How many terms are inside the parentheses? How many products should distributing give?
Which route is easier here -- divide first or distribute first?
Did the outside number reach the second term?
What do you get if you check your answer in the original?
Do both routes give the same solution?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student distributes to the first term only (writes px + q = r).
misconception_redirects.say: If you distribute, draw an arrow from the outside number to EACH term inside and say both products aloud. If you divide first, divide the whole right side by p before you touch the parentheses.
misconception_redirects.praise: You multiplied both terms (or divided the whole side) -- that's a clean parenthesis solve.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student divides the parenthesis side by p but not the right side.
misconception_redirects.say: Whatever you do to the left, do to the right. If you divide the left by p, divide r by p too.
misconception_redirects.praise: You divided BOTH sides by p -- the equation stays balanced.

quick_checks.look_for: x = 3 (divide by 5 -> x + 1 = 4). Distributing to only the first term (5x + 1 = 20) gives 3.8 -- a red flag.

sentence_starters: I can divide both sides by ___ first, which gives ___.
If I distribute, ___ times x is ___ and ___ times ___ is ___.

steps.annotation: The variable is inside parentheses; I will divide first.
Dividing by 0.5 is doubling: 7.5 / 0.5 = 15.
Undo the -3 to isolate x.
Both sides match, so x = 18.
I will distribute the 4 to each term.
4 times x = 4x AND 4 times 3 = 12 -- both terms.
Subtract 12 from both sides to clear the constant.
Divide by 4, then check by substituting back.

skills.name: Identify the equation that models a real-world situation
skills.i_do_script: Before I can solve a word problem I have to build the right equation, and that means giving every number a JOB. Watch the spec's example: a crew already set up 250 chairs and adds 75 chairs each hour; they need 550 total. The 75 is a RATE -- it happens each hour -- so it multiplies the hours: 75h. The 250 is a one-time amount that is added on: + 250. The total 550 is what it all equals. So the equation is 75h + 250 = 550. The rate multiplies the variable; the one-time amount stands alone.

canonical_error.pattern: Swaps the roles of the per-unit rate and the one-time amount (or attaches the rate to the wrong number)
canonical_error.example: For '250 chairs set up, 75 added per hour, 550 total' the student writes 75 + 250h = 550, multiplying the one-time amount by the variable
canonical_error.why: The student matches numbers to slots by the order they appear rather than by meaning. The RATE (per hour/per item) multiplies the variable; the fixed one-time amount is added on its own.

skills.item_template: A real-world situation; student selects the equation of the form px + q = r (or p(x + q) = r) that models it. Multiple choice.

sample_items.stem:
A crew has already set up 250 chairs and sets up 75 more chairs each hour. A total of 550 chairs are needed.

Which equation can be used to find h, the number of hours?
sample_items.distractor_logic: The rate 75 multiplies the hours and 250 is added once. '75 + 250h = 550' swaps the roles; the '325' options add the numbers before modeling.

sample_items.stem:
A taxi charges a $3 flat fee plus $2 per mile. A ride costs $17.

Which equation finds m, the number of miles?
sample_items.distractor_logic: The $2 per mile multiplies m; the $3 fee is added once. '3m + 2' swaps them; '5m' adds the numbers first.

sample_items.stem:
A savings account starts at $20 and grows $5 each week.

Which equation finds w, the weeks to reach $65?
sample_items.distractor_logic: The $5 weekly rate multiplies w; the $20 start is added once. The others swap or combine the numbers.

sample_items.stem:
A gym charges a $30 sign-up fee plus $8 per month. The total paid is $70.

Which equation finds m, the number of months?
sample_items.distractor_logic: The $8/month rate multiplies m; the $30 fee is once. '30m + 8' and '8 + 30m' swap roles; '38m' combines first.

redirect_script.stop: Which number happens over and over?
redirect_script.prompt: Label the RATE (the 'per hour/per item' number) -- it multiplies the variable. Label the ONE-TIME amount -- it is added on its own. Write each number's job before you pick an equation.
redirect_script.praise: You put the rate on the variable and the one-time amount on its own -- correct modeling.

vocabulary.definition: Turn the words of a situation into an equation.
A per-unit amount (per hour, per mile) that multiplies the variable.
A letter standing for the unknown you are solving for.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'A pool holds 30 gallons and fills 10 gallons per minute; it needs 90 gallons. Find m.'
Which number is per minute? Which is the starting amount?
10 is per minute, so 10m; 30 is the start, added once; 90 is the total. Equation: 10m + 30 = 90.
If a student writes 30m + 10 = 90, ask 'which number repeats every minute?'
Your turn: a $5 entry plus $2 per ride, total $19 -- write the equation for rides r.

practice_problems.stem: A gym charges $5 per class. Write an expression for the cost of x classes.
In the equation 8x + 20 = 60, which number is the one-time (fixed) amount?
practice_problems.answer: 20 (the constant). The 8 is the per-unit rate.

practice_problems.stem: A crew set up 250 chairs and adds 75 per hour; 550 are needed. Which equation finds the hours h: (a) 325h = 550  (b) 75h + 250 = 550  (c) 250h + 75 = 550  (d) 75 + 250h = 550?
practice_problems.notes: Spec's Approaching example.

practice_problems.stem: A taxi charges a $3 fee plus $2 per mile; a ride cost $17. Write the equation for miles m.
Taylor modeled 'a $4 entry fee plus $6 per ride, total $28' as an equation. Find and fix it.
shown_work: where x is the number of rides.
practice_problems.answer: Taylor put the one-time $4 fee on the variable and the $6 rate on its own. The $6 is per ride, so it multiplies x: 6x + 4 = 28. (Then x = 4 rides.)
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: swapped the rate and the fixed amount.

practice_problems.stem: A savings account starts at $20 and grows $5 per week. Write the equation for the weeks w to reach $65.
Write a real-world situation that the equation 3x + 10 = 40 could model.
practice_problems.answer: Sample: a $10 flat fee plus $3 per item, x items, totaling $40.
practice_problems.notes: Reverse direction -- invent a context for a given equation.

practice_problems.stem: A phone plan is $15 plus $0.10 per text and totals $25. A classmate writes 15x + 0.10 = 25. Explain the error and write the correct equation.
practice_problems.answer: The $0.10 is per text, so it multiplies x; the $15 is once: 0.10x + 15 = 25 (x = 100 texts). The classmate swapped the rate and the fixed fee.
practice_problems.notes: Critique-and-correct with a decimal rate.

activities.title: Rate or One-Time?
activities.instructions:
1. Each card names a number from a story, like '$75 per hour' or '250 chairs already set up.'
2. Sort each card into 'Multiplies the variable (rate)' or 'Added once (one-time amount).'
3. Rule: if the number happens per hour/per item, it multiplies the variable; if it happens once, it is added on its own.
4. Pick two rate cards and two one-time cards and build one equation from them.
5. Debrief: how do you tell a rate from a one-time amount?

activities.title: Whose Job Is That Number?
activities.instructions:
1. Read Taylor's equation 4x + 6 = 28 for 'a $4 entry fee plus $6 per ride.'
2. Underline the one-time fee and circle the per-ride rate in the words.
3. Rewrite the equation with each number in the right job.
4. Write a rule for deciding which number multiplies the variable.

content.worked_problem: A $4 entry fee plus $6 per ride (x rides) totals $28. Taylor wrote 4x + 6 = 28.
content.error_step: Taylor multiplied the one-time $4 fee by x and left the $6 rate alone.
content.why: The $4 happens once (constant) and the $6 is per ride (multiplies x): 6x + 4 = 28, x = 4.

strategy_links.why: The swapped-roles error is a clean, high-frequency modeling mistake for a find-and-fix routine.
Think-pair-share on 'what is each number's job?' surfaces the rate-vs-fixed distinction through talk.
A journal entry naming what each number does cements mapping by meaning rather than word order.

questioning_prompts: What are you solving for? Give it a letter.
Which number happens over and over (a rate)? Which happens once?
What does each number in your equation stand for in the story?
Where should the rate go -- on the variable or by itself?
Does your equation match every part of the situation?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student puts the one-time fee on the variable and the per-unit rate on its own.
misconception_redirects.say: Label the RATE (the 'per hour/per item' number) -- it multiplies the variable. Label the ONE-TIME amount -- it is added on its own. Write each number's job before you pick an equation.
misconception_redirects.praise: You put the rate on the variable and the one-time amount on its own -- correct modeling.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student combines the two numbers before modeling (e.g., 325h = 550).
misconception_redirects.say: Keep the rate and the one-time amount separate -- don't add them together first. One multiplies the variable; the other is added after.
misconception_redirects.praise: You kept the rate and the fixed amount as separate parts -- that's the right structure.

quick_checks.prompt: A $4 fee plus $3 per game, total $19. Write the equation for games g.
$50 saved plus $10 per week to reach $120. Write the equation for weeks w.
quick_checks.look_for: 10w + 50 = 120. Putting 50 on w (50w + 10) is the role swap.

sentence_starters: The number ___ happens per ___, so it multiplies the variable.
The number ___ happens once, so I add it on its own.

worked_solution.stem: A pool holds 30 gallons and fills at 10 gallons per minute. Write the equation to find m, the minutes to reach 90 gallons.

steps.annotation: The rate happens every minute, so it multiplies the variable m.
A one-time starting amount, added on its own.
Everything equals the target total.
Rate on the variable, one-time amount alone, total on the right.

faded_example.stem: A savings account has $20 and grows $5 per week. Write the equation to find w, the weeks to reach $65.

steps.annotation: The weekly rate multiplies the variable w.
A one-time amount, added alone.
Write '= 65' for the target total.
Put the three pieces together into one equation.

skills.name: Write and solve an equation for a real-world problem
skills.i_do_script: Now I both BUILD the equation and SOLVE it. Watch the spec's example: a class has 8 boys and x girls, and each of the students has 4 pencils, for 52 pencils total. The whole group is (x + 8) students, and each has 4 pencils, so 4(x + 8) = 52. I solve by dividing first: x + 8 = 13, then subtract 8 to get x = 5 girls. I check: 4(5 + 8) = 4(13) = 52. When the rate applies to a WHOLE group, the parentheses hold the whole group.

canonical_error.pattern: Multiplies the rate by only the unknown, leaving the known part of the group out of the parentheses
canonical_error.example: For 'x girls and 8 boys, 4 pencils each, 52 total' the student writes 4x + 8 = 52 instead of 4(x + 8) = 52
canonical_error.why: The student attaches the rate to the variable alone and forgets the rate applies to the ENTIRE group. The 4 pencils are per student, and there are (x + 8) students, so the 4 multiplies the whole sum.

skills.item_template: A real-world situation leading to p(x + q) = r or px + q = r with whole-number values. Student writes the equation (Part A) and solves it (Part B). Multi-part response.

sample_items.stem:
A class has 8 boys and x girls. Each student has 4 pencils. The total number of pencils is 52.

Part A: Write an equation that models the situation.
Part B: How many girls are in the class?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Whole group (x + 8) at 4 pencils each: 4(x + 8) = 52, x = 5. Writing 4x + 8 = 52 forgets the rate applies to the boys too.

sample_items.stem:
A booster club buys x adult shirts and 6 kid shirts. Each shirt costs $15. They spend $180.

Part A: Write an equation.
Part B: How many adult shirts?
sample_items.answer: Part A: 15(x + 6) = 180 (or 15x + 90 = 180); Part B: x = 6 adult shirts

sample_items.stem:
A gym charges a $10 sign-up fee plus $8 per month. A member paid $50 total.

Part A: Write an equation for the months m.
Part B: How many months?
sample_items.answer: Part A: 8m + 10 = 50; Part B: m = 5 months

sample_items.stem:
A store sells x adult tickets and 5 child tickets, each $9. The total is $135.

Part A: Write an equation.
Part B: How many adult tickets?

redirect_script.stop: Does the rate apply to the WHOLE group?
redirect_script.prompt: Ask who the per-item amount covers. If every person or item in the group gets it, put the whole group in parentheses: rate times (unknown + known). Then divide by the rate first.
redirect_script.praise: You put the whole group in the parentheses -- the rate reaches everyone, not just x.

vocabulary.definition: Write the situation as an equation.
The whole set the rate applies to, like all (x + 8) students.
Different-looking equations with the same solution, like 4(x + 8) = 52 and 4x + 32 = 52.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'A booth has x new chairs plus 3 old chairs. Each seats 2 people; 20 seats total. Find x.'
How many chairs are there in all? What does each chair provide?
There are (x + 3) chairs, each seats 2: 2(x + 3) = 20. Divide by 2: x + 3 = 10, so x = 7.
If a student writes 2x + 3 = 20, ask 'do the OLD chairs seat people too?'
Your turn: 4 boys and x girls, 3 stickers each, 27 total -- write and solve.

practice_problems.stem: A class has 8 boys and x girls. Write an expression for the total number of students.
Solve 4(x + 8) = 52.
A class has 8 boys and x girls; each student has 4 pencils; 52 pencils total. Part A: write an equation. Part B: how many girls?
practice_problems.notes: Spec's At example; rate applies to the whole group.

practice_problems.stem: A booster club buys x adult shirts and 6 kid shirts, each $15, spending $180. Write and solve for x.
Sam modeled the pencil problem (8 boys, x girls, 4 pencils each, 52 total). Find and fix the equation.
practice_problems.answer: Sam gave pencils to the girls only. Every student -- all (x + 8) of them -- has 4 pencils: 4(x + 8) = 52, so x + 8 = 13 and x = 5 girls. Check: 4(5 + 8) = 52.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: rate left off the known part of the group.

practice_problems.stem: A gym charges a $10 sign-up fee plus $8 per month; total paid $50. Write and solve for the months m.
practice_problems.notes: px + q = r form (rate on the variable, one fee).

practice_problems.stem: A store sells x adult tickets and 5 child tickets at $9 each for $135. Write TWO equivalent equations, then solve.
practice_problems.notes: Two forms of the same model (previews S6).

practice_problems.stem: Write your own word problem that leads to 6(x + 4) = 60, then solve it.
practice_problems.answer: Sample: 'x new plus 4 old benches, each seating 6, seat 60 people.' x = 6.
practice_problems.notes: Reverse direction -- build a story for an equation.

activities.title: Build It, Solve It, Check It
activities.instructions:
1. Draw a context card, like '8 boys and x girls, 4 pencils each, 52 total.'
2. On the sheet, write the whole group as (unknown + known), then the rate, then build rate times (group) = total.
3. Solve by dividing by the rate first.
4. Check by substituting your answer back and confirming the total.
5. Trade sheets; a partner only accepts the answer if the check reproduces the total.
6. Debrief: how do you know whether the rate covers the whole group?

activities.title: Who Gets the Rate?
activities.instructions:
1. Read Sam's equation 4x + 8 = 52 for the pencil problem.
2. Decide who the 4 pencils actually belong to -- just the girls, or every student?
3. Rewrite the equation so the rate covers the whole group, then solve.
4. Discuss: how could the strange answer (11 girls) have warned Sam something was off?

content.worked_problem: 8 boys and x girls, 4 pencils each, 52 total. Sam wrote 4x + 8 = 52 and got x = 11.
content.error_step: Sam multiplied 4 by the girls only, adding the 8 boys as a loose constant.
content.why: Every student has 4 pencils, so 4(x + 8) = 52, giving x = 5 girls.

strategy_links.why: Build-then-solve is a natural gradual-release script: model the equation, then hand off the solving.
Drawing the whole group (boxes for each person/item) makes it concrete that the rate covers everyone.
The rate-left-off-the-group error is precise and high-value for a find-and-fix routine.

questioning_prompts: Who or what does the per-item rate apply to -- just x, or the whole group?
How would you write the size of the whole group?
Which route solves it faster -- divide by the rate first, or distribute?
What does your answer mean in the story, and is it sensible?
Does the total check when you substitute back?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student writes rate times x plus known instead of rate times (x + known).
misconception_redirects.say: Ask who the per-item amount covers. If every person or item in the group gets it, put the whole group in parentheses: rate times (unknown + known). Then divide by the rate first.
misconception_redirects.praise: You put the whole group in the parentheses -- the rate reaches everyone, not just x.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student writes the equation correctly but stops without solving Part B or checking.
misconception_redirects.say: Part B wants a number. Divide by the rate, isolate x, then substitute back to make sure the total matches.
misconception_redirects.praise: You carried the model all the way to a checked answer -- that's the full task.

quick_checks.prompt: 6 red pens and x blue pens, $2 each, $20 total. Write the equation.
quick_checks.look_for: 2(x + 6) = 20 (or 2x + 12 = 20). Writing 2x + 6 = 20 leaves the red pens out of the rate.

quick_checks.prompt: Solve your equation for the number of blue pens.
quick_checks.look_for: x = 4. An answer of 7 (from 2x + 6 = 20) signals the missing-group error.

sentence_starters: The whole group is (___ + ___), and each gets ___, so my equation is ___.
Solving, x = ___, which means ___ in the story.

worked_solution.stem: A class has 8 boys and x girls. Each student has 4 pencils, and there are 52 pencils in all. How many girls?

steps.annotation: The rate (4 pencils) applies to the WHOLE group, so the group goes in parentheses.
Undo the multiplication that covers the group.
Clear the known part to find the unknown.
5 girls -- a sensible whole number, and the total checks.

faded_example.stem: A booth has x new chairs plus 3 old chairs. Each chair seats 2 people, for 20 seats total. How many new chairs?

steps.annotation: The rate covers all the chairs, new and old.
Undo the times 2 on the whole group.
Subtract 3 to isolate x.
Check by putting your answer back into the story.

skills.name: Write and solve a real-world problem with rational-number values
skills.i_do_script: This is the same modeling as before, but now the numbers are fractions or decimals -- so I have to keep the arithmetic clean. Watch the spec's example: a baker uses 3 cups of flour for bread and 1.5 cups for each batch of cookies, using 12 cups total. The 1.5 is per batch, so it multiplies x: 1.5x; the 3 cups is a one-time amount: + 3; the total is 12. So 1.5x + 3 = 12. I subtract 3 to get 1.5x = 9, then divide by 1.5 to get x = 6 batches. Dividing by 1.5 is the step people skip -- I never leave the coefficient attached.

canonical_error.pattern: Clears the constant but then fails to divide by the fractional or decimal coefficient (or divides incorrectly)
canonical_error.example: For 1.5x + 3 = 12 the student gets 1.5x = 9 and then writes x = 9, forgetting to divide by 1.5
canonical_error.why: The student treats a decimal or fraction coefficient as if it were a 1, stopping a step early. The variable is still multiplied by 1.5, so both sides must be divided by 1.5 to finish.

skills.item_template: A real-world situation leading to px + q = r or p(x + q) = r with at least one fraction or decimal. Student writes the equation (Part A) and solves it (Part B). Multi-part response.

sample_items.stem:
A baker uses 3 cups of flour for bread and 1.5 cups for each batch of cookies, using 12 cups total.

Part A: Write an equation, with x the number of batches.
Part B: How many batches can the baker make?
sample_items.answer: Part A: 1.5x + 3 = 12; Part B: x = 6 batches
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1.5 per batch times x, plus 3 for bread, equals 12. Subtract 3 (1.5x = 9), divide by 1.5 -> 6. Forgetting to divide by 1.5 leaves x = 9.

sample_items.stem:
A plumber charges $12.50 per hour plus a $5 trip fee. The bill is $67.50.

Part A: Write an equation for the hours h.
Part B: How many hours?
sample_items.answer: Part A: 12.5h + 5 = 67.5; Part B: h = 5 hours

sample_items.stem:
A 5-yard ribbon is cut into pieces 3/4 yard long, with 1/2 yard left over.

Part A: Write an equation for the number of pieces x.
Part B: How many pieces?
sample_items.answer: Part A: (3/4)x + 1/2 = 5; Part B: x = 6 pieces

sample_items.stem:
A gym charges $19.99 per month plus a one-time $25 fee. A member paid $84.97.

Part A: Write an equation for the months m.
Part B: How many months?
sample_items.answer: Part A: 19.99m + 25 = 84.97; Part B: m = 3 months

redirect_script.stop: You are not done -- is x still multiplied?
redirect_script.prompt: After you clear the constant, look at the number stuck to x. If it is a fraction or decimal, divide BOTH sides by it (a calculator is allowed). Only x, alone, means you are finished.
redirect_script.praise: You divided out the decimal coefficient -- that's the last step people skip.

vocabulary.definition: A fraction, decimal, or whole number.
The number multiplied by the variable, like 1.5 in 1.5x.
Solving accurately and efficiently, even with fractions and decimals.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'Cases cost $7.50 each; flat shipping is $5; an order totaled $35. How many cases?'
Which number is per case? Which is one-time?
7.50 per case is 7.5x; the $5 shipping is added once; total 35: 7.5x + 5 = 35. Subtract 5: 7.5x = 30. Divide by 7.5: x = 4.
If a student stops at 7.5x = 30 and says x = 30, ask 'is x by itself yet?'
Your turn: $1.50 per batch plus 3 cups, total 12 -- write and solve.

practice_problems.stem: A baker uses 1.5 cups of flour per batch. Write an expression for x batches.
Solve 1.5x = 9.
A baker uses 3 cups for bread and 1.5 cups per batch of cookies, 12 cups total. Part A: write an equation. Part B: how many batches?
practice_problems.answer: Part A: 1.5x + 3 = 12; Part B: x = 6 batches
practice_problems.notes: Spec's At (medium) example; divide by 1.5 to finish.

practice_problems.stem: A plumber charges $12.50 per hour plus a $5 trip fee; the bill is $67.50. Write and solve for hours h.
Jamie solved 1.5x + 3 = 12. Find and fix the mistake.
practice_problems.answer: Jamie stopped a step early -- x is still multiplied by 1.5. Divide both sides by 1.5: x = 6. Check: 1.5(6) + 3 = 12.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: not dividing by the decimal coefficient.

practice_problems.stem: A 5-yard ribbon is cut into 3/4-yard pieces with 1/2 yard left over. Write and solve for the number of pieces x.
practice_problems.notes: Fraction coefficient and constant.

practice_problems.stem: A gym charges $19.99 per month plus a one-time $25 fee; a member paid $84.97. Write and solve for the months m.
practice_problems.notes: Decimals to the hundredth; a calculator is allowed.

practice_problems.stem: Write a real-world problem that leads to 0.25x + 2 = 5, then solve it.
practice_problems.answer: Sample: '$2 base plus $0.25 per token, total $5, x tokens.' x = 12.
practice_problems.notes: Reverse direction with a decimal rate.

activities.title: Set Up, Then Finish the Divide
activities.instructions:
1. Draw a context card with a fraction or decimal rate (like the baker's 1.5 cups).
2. In 'Set up,' write the equation (rate times x plus one-time amount = total).
3. In 'Solve,' clear the constant, THEN divide by the fraction/decimal coefficient -- you may use a calculator.
4. Circle the final answer only after x stands alone, and check by substituting back.
5. Debrief: what is the last step people forget when the coefficient is a decimal?

activities.title: Finish the Divide
activities.instructions:
1. Read Jamie's solve of 1.5x + 3 = 12 that ends at 'x = 9.'
2. Ask: after 1.5x = 9, is x by itself yet?
3. Do the missing step (divide by 1.5) and check your answer.
4. Write a reminder for yourself about decimal or fraction coefficients.

content.error_step: Jamie stopped without dividing by the 1.5 still multiplying x.
content.why: Divide both sides by 1.5: x = 6. A calculator is allowed, so there is no excuse to skip the divide.

strategy_links.why: The stopped-early (no final divide) error is precise and common with decimal coefficients -- ideal for find-and-fix.
Thinking aloud 'is x by itself yet?' models the self-check that catches the missing divide.
Gradual release lets students set up first, then practice finishing the rational-coefficient divide independently.

questioning_prompts: Which number is per unit (the coefficient), and which is one-time?
After you clear the constant, is x by itself yet?
What do you divide both sides by to finish?
Would a calculator help you trust the decimal step?
Does your answer make sense as a count in this story?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student clears the constant but leaves x multiplied by a decimal or fraction.
misconception_redirects.say: After you clear the constant, look at the number stuck to x. If it is a fraction or decimal, divide BOTH sides by it (a calculator is allowed). Only x, alone, means you are finished.
misconception_redirects.praise: You divided out the decimal coefficient -- that's the last step people skip.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student mishandles the decimal arithmetic (e.g., 67.5 - 5 wrong).
misconception_redirects.say: Slow the arithmetic down and use the calculator you are allowed. Line up the decimals: 67.5 - 5 = 62.5.
misconception_redirects.praise: You kept the decimal arithmetic accurate -- fluency includes trusting the numbers.

quick_checks.look_for: x = 4 (2.5x = 10, then divide by 2.5). Stopping at 2.5x = 10 and saying x = 10 is the missing-divide error.

quick_checks.prompt: A $6 fee plus $0.50 per mile totals $10. Solve for miles m.
quick_checks.look_for: m = 8 (0.5m = 4, divide by 0.5). An answer of 4 means the student skipped dividing by 0.5.

sentence_starters: The one-time amount is ___ and the per-unit rate is ___, so my equation is ___.
After I subtract ___, x is still times ___, so I divide to get x = ___.

worked_solution.stem: A baker uses 3 cups of flour for bread and 1.5 cups per batch of cookies, using 12 cups total. How many batches?

steps.annotation: 1.5 cups per batch times x, plus 3 cups for bread, equals 12.
Clear the one-time amount first.
x was multiplied by 1.5, so divide both sides by 1.5 (a calculator is allowed).
6 batches -- the total checks.

faded_example.stem: Phone cases cost $7.50 each and shipping is a flat $5. An order totaled $35. How many cases?

steps.annotation: 7.50 per case times x, plus $5 shipping, equals 35.
Clear the one-time shipping first.
x is still times 7.5 -- divide both sides by 7.5.
Check by substituting your answer back.

skills.name: Represent a problem with more than one equivalent equation and compare methods
skills.i_do_script: At the top level I can model ONE situation with more than one correct equation and know they are equivalent, and I can judge whether an answer is reasonable. Watch the spec's example: a shopper buys 5 red shirts and x blue shirts, each $9.50, for $76. One equation groups all the shirts: 9.50(x + 5) = 76. Another distributes the price: 9.50x + 47.50 = 76. Both are correct because distributing 9.50(x + 5) gives 9.50x + 47.50 -- same equation, different form. Both solve to x = 3. To judge reasonableness I check: 3 blue plus 5 red is 8 shirts at $9.50 is $76. It fits.

canonical_error.pattern: Treats the grouped and distributed forms as different equations, or distributes incorrectly so the two forms are not truly equivalent
canonical_error.example: Calls 9.50(x + 5) = 76 and 9.50x + 5 = 76 equivalent -- the second forgot to multiply 5 by 9.50 (it should be 47.50)
canonical_error.why: The student does not connect p(x + q) with px + pq, or distributes only the first term. Two equations are equivalent only when one distributes exactly into the other and both share the same solution.

skills.item_template: A real-world situation; student writes or selects TWO equivalent equations, compares two solution methods, or judges whether a stated solution is reasonable. Multiple-select or multi-part response.

sample_items.stem: A shopper buys 5 red shirts and x blue shirts at $9.50 each for $76. Write the TWO equivalent equations that model this.
sample_items.distractor_logic: The grouped form 9.50(x + 5) = 76 distributes exactly into 9.50x + 47.50 = 76. '9.50x + 5 = 76' forgets to multiply the 5 by 9.50, so it is NOT equivalent.

sample_items.stem: A booth sells x student tickets and 4 adult tickets at $7 each for $84 total. Write two equivalent equations for x, then solve.
A linear equation is 3(x - 2) = 9. Student A distributes first; Student B divides both sides by 3 first. Do the two methods give the same solution? Solve both ways.
A student solved 5(x + 2) = 45 and got x = 11. Is that reasonable? Check it and correct it if needed.
sample_items.answer: No -- 5(11 + 2) = 5(13) = 65, not 45. The correct solution is x = 7, since 5(7 + 2) = 5(9) = 45.

redirect_script.stop: Are those two equations really the same?
redirect_script.prompt: Distribute the grouped form on scratch paper: p(x + q) becomes px + pq. If your two equations don't match after distributing -- or don't share the same solution -- they aren't equivalent. Check that every term got multiplied.
redirect_script.praise: You showed the two forms distribute into each other AND share a solution -- truly equivalent.

vocabulary.definition: Equations with the same solution; one distributes exactly into the other.
Multiply the outside factor by every term inside the parentheses.
An answer that actually fits the situation when you check it.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for 8.AF.1 (multi-step equations, variables on both sides).

worked_example_script.text: Write 'A team buys x new balls and 3 spares at $6 each, $54 total.'
What is one equation that groups all the balls?
6(x + 3) = 54. Distribute it: 6x + 18 = 54 -- a second, equivalent equation. Both solve to x = 6.
If a student writes 6x + 3 = 54, ask 'what is 6 times 3?'
Your turn: 5 red and x blue shirts at $9.50, total $76 -- write both forms.

practice_problems.stem: Show that 3(x + 4) and 3x + 12 are equal by testing x = 2.
Distribute: 9.50(x + 5).
A shopper buys 5 red shirts and x blue shirts at $9.50 each for $76. Write the TWO equivalent equations that model this.
practice_problems.notes: Spec's Above example; grouped and distributed forms.

practice_problems.stem: 3(x - 2) = 9. Student A distributes first; Student B divides by 3 first. Do they get the same solution? Solve both ways.
practice_problems.notes: Spec's Above compare-methods item.

practice_problems.stem: Riley says 6(x + 3) = 48 and 6x + 3 = 48 are the same equation. Find and fix the error.
shown_work: Riley wrote: '6(x + 3) = 48 is the same as 6x + 3 = 48.'
practice_problems.answer: Distributing 6(x + 3) gives 6x + 18, not 6x + 3. The equivalent form is 6x + 18 = 48, which solves to x = 5 (matching 6(x + 3) = 48). Riley multiplied only the first term.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: incomplete distribution breaks equivalence.

practice_problems.stem: A booth sells x student tickets and 4 adult tickets at $7 each for $84. Write two equivalent equations, then solve.
practice_problems.notes: Both forms, then solve.

practice_problems.stem: A number is multiplied by 4, then 6 is added, giving 30. Solve it algebraically (write an equation) and arithmetically (work backward). Which operations does each method use, and in what order?
practice_problems.answer: Algebraic: 4x + 6 = 30 -> 4x = 24 -> x = 6. Arithmetic: undo the +6 (30 - 6 = 24), then undo the times 4 (24 / 4 = 6). Both use subtraction then division, in the same order.
practice_problems.notes: Compare algebraic and arithmetic approaches (Above descriptor).

practice_problems.stem: A student solved 5(x + 2) = 45 and got x = 11. Is that reasonable? Check, and correct if needed.
practice_problems.notes: Judge reasonableness and correct (Above descriptor).

activities.title: Same Equation, Two Forms
materials: Card set: 6 grouped-form cards and 8 distributed-form cards (two incomplete-distribution decoys)
activities.instructions:
1. Match each grouped form p(x + q) to its correct distributed form.
2. Two distributed cards are decoys that multiplied only the first term -- set them aside and name why they are NOT equivalent.
3. To claim a match, show that distributing gives every term.
4. Pick one matched pair and solve both forms to confirm the same answer.
5. Debrief: what has to be true for two equations to be equivalent?

activities.title: Is It Really Equivalent?
activities.instructions:
1. Read Riley's claim that 6(x + 3) = 48 and 6x + 3 = 48 are the same.
2. Distribute 6(x + 3) fully -- what should the constant term be?
3. Solve both of Riley's equations and show their solutions differ.
4. Write the two-part test for equivalence: distributes exactly AND same solution.

content.error_step: Riley multiplied 6 by x but not by the 3 inside.
content.why: 6(x + 3) = 6x + 18, so the equivalent form is 6x + 18 = 48 (x = 5). Riley's 6x + 3 = 48 gives x = 7.5 -- a different equation.

strategy_links.why: Comparing a correct equivalence against an incomplete-distribution version is exactly a correct-vs-incorrect worked-example routine.
The false-equivalence error is a precise, high-value mistake for a find-and-fix routine.
Writing WHY two forms are equivalent (or why an answer is reasonable) cements the justification the Above band demands.

questioning_prompts: What is one equation that groups everything? What is another that distributes it?
How can you PROVE two equations are equivalent?
Do both solution methods land on the same answer?
Is the answer reasonable -- does it fit the situation when you check?
Which method was more efficient here, and why?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student treats a grouped form and an incompletely distributed form as equivalent.
misconception_redirects.say: Distribute the grouped form on scratch paper: p(x + q) becomes px + pq. If your two equations don't match after distributing -- or don't share the same solution -- they aren't equivalent. Check that every term got multiplied.
misconception_redirects.praise: You showed the two forms distribute into each other AND share a solution -- truly equivalent.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student accepts an answer without judging whether it is reasonable.
misconception_redirects.say: Put the answer back into the story and check the total. If the numbers don't fit -- like paying more than the total -- the answer isn't reasonable.
misconception_redirects.praise: You checked the answer against the situation -- that's judging reasonableness.

quick_checks.look_for: 8x + 16. Writing 8x + 2 (forgetting to multiply the 2) is the equivalence-breaking error.

quick_checks.prompt: A student says x = 10 solves 4(x + 1) = 24. Reasonable?
quick_checks.look_for: No -- 4(11) = 44, not 24; the correct x = 5. A 'yes' means they didn't check.

sentence_starters: The grouped form is ___ and the distributed form is ___; they are equivalent because ___.

worked_solution.stem: A shopper buys 5 red shirts and x blue shirts at $9.50 each for $76. Write two equivalent equations and solve.

steps.annotation: All (x + 5) shirts cost $9.50 each.
Distribute: 9.50 times x and 9.50 times 5 = 47.50 -- an equivalent equation.
Either form gives the same solution.
8 shirts at $9.50 is $76 -- reasonable.

faded_example.stem: A team buys x new balls and 3 spare balls at $6 each for $54. Write two equivalent equations and solve.

steps.annotation: All (x + 3) balls at $6 each.
6 times x and 6 times 3 = 18 -- equivalent.
Solve either form: subtract 18, then divide by 6.
Check: substitute your answer and confirm the total is $54.

looking_back.label: Looking Back
looking_back.description: Skills the student should have but may need re-teaching.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S4 (write and solve a real-world equation) -- the At-proficiency core of the standard. If they pass, push to S5 (rational-number contexts) and S6 (multiple equivalent equations and reasonableness). If they fail, split the diagnosis: S1 checks whether they can solve px + q = r, S2 whether they can solve p(x + q) = r, and S3 whether they can translate a situation into the right equation. S6 also branches off the top of the application side.
